name: Dimethylcurcumin (ASC-J9)

lead: ASC-J9 (dimethylcurcumin) is an experimental curcumin-derived compound that has drawn interest as a topical acne approach. Instead of just blocking the androgen receptor, it lowers the amount of receptor protein in cells.

The idea is less androgen-driven oil and inflammation in skin, and so fewer breakouts. Two Phase 2 acne trials of a cream (2007 and 2011, around 180 participants each) are registered as completed, but no published results were found. Most other work is laboratory and animal research on conditions such as prostate cancer.

paras: It has been tested as a topical cream in clinical trials and is not available as an approved product, so there is no established routine for using it.
It is experimental and not approved by regulators. Human safety data from the acne trials are not published in the sources reviewed; most other data come from cell and animal studies.

angle.text: ASC-J9 aims at acne by reducing androgen receptor protein in skin, which should mean less oil and inflammation and fewer breakouts. It reached two Phase 2 acne cream trials, but no results were found.

lead: Dimethylcurcumin, known by the development code ASC-J9 (and also GO-Y025), is a synthetic curcumin derivative described as a nonsteroidal antiandrogen. Unlike conventional androgen receptor (AR) blockers, it is reported to work by promoting degradation of the androgen receptor protein rather than only occupying the receptor.[1][2] It is listed as an experimental drug and is not approved for any use.[1]

In appearance-related contexts it has been of interest as a topical anti-androgen for acne. Two Phase 2 trials of an ASC-J9 cream in acne were registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, one starting in 2007 with 186 participants and one in 2011 with 181 participants.[3][4] Both are listed as completed, but no peer-reviewed results for them are among the sources reviewed for this article, so its effect on acne in humans is not established in the published literature found here.

Most published work on ASC-J9 is laboratory and animal research, led by the group of Chawnshang Chang, in areas such as prostate cancer, spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy, bladder and liver cancer models, and wound healing.[5][6][7][8]

paras: Wikipedia describes ASC-J9 as inhibiting the androgen receptor in vitro without being a conventional antagonist; instead it appears to enhance AR degradation, apparently acting on particular AR populations.[1] A 2007 Nature Medicine paper reported that it reduced AR protein levels and improved the phenotype in a mouse model of spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy.[6] Later preclinical papers reported it degrading both full-length and splice-variant androgen receptors in castration-resistant prostate cancer cell models.[9][2]

Because it targets AR protein levels in tissues where AR is expressed, researchers have proposed that it could act locally in skin when applied topically, which is the rationale for the acne studies; this is a hypothesis about the design of the trials rather than a demonstrated result.

Two Phase 2 trials of topical ASC-J9 cream in acne are registered: NCT00525499 (acne vulgaris, started August 2007, 186 participants) and NCT01289574 (acne, started February 2011, 181 participants). Both are listed as completed.[3][4] No published results from either trial were found among the sources reviewed, so no efficacy or safety figures can be reported here.

Preclinical studies attribute a range of effects to AR signaling that ASC-J9 is used to probe. In mice, AR deletion or suppression has been linked to altered bladder cancer development, liver cancer development, hepatitis B-related liver tumour formation, and cutaneous wound healing speed.[5][7][8][10] Studies in prostate cancer models reported that ASC-J9 and the clinically used AR antagonists enzalutamide and bicalutamide had opposite effects on metastasis-related macrophage signaling.[11] These are animal and cell findings and have not been established in people.
ASC-J9 has also been tested in preclinical models of benign prostatic hyperplasia-related AR biology and in enzalutamide-resistant prostate cancer models.[9][12]

timeline.event: Nature Medicine paper reports ASC-J9 reduces AR protein in a spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy mouse model.[6]
Phase 2 trial of ASC-J9 cream in acne vulgaris begins (NCT00525499).[4]
